vopros: What do foreign nationals need to buy a home in Los Angeles?

vyzhimka.tekst:
Yes. A foreign national generally can buy a home in Los Angeles without being a U.S. citizen or permanent resident. There is no general California residency requirement to own residential real estate. The bigger differences are financing, documentation, taxes, and how you hold title.

For a typical purchase, you'll need:

- Identification: usually a valid passport and sometimes a second government-issued ID.
- Purchase funds: enough for the deposit/down payment, closing costs, and any lender-required reserves. Escrow and banks will also require documentation showing where the money came from, particularly for international wire transfers.
- U.S. bank account: not legally required simply to own property, but often useful and sometimes effectively necessary for financing, escrow, taxes, insurance, and ongoing expenses.
- ITIN/SSN: you don't necessarily need an SSN merely to purchase a property. An ITIN can become important for U.S. tax filings and later transactions. California specifically notes that foreign property sellers who lack a TIN may need to obtain an ITIN to claim certain withholding exemptions. ([ftb.ca.gov](https://www.ftb.ca.gov/forms/misc/1016.html?utm_source=openai))
- Financing documentation: if you're getting a mortgage, expect substantially more documentation than a U.S. borrower might provide. Foreign-national mortgage programs often evaluate foreign income/assets, passports/visas, bank statements, credit references, and reserves. Some buyers instead purchase entirely with cash.
- Homeowners insurance and normal closing documents: essentially the same basic process as for domestic buyers.

One important point: buying a house does not itself give you U.S. immigration status, a visa, or the right to live in the United States.

Taxes also deserve attention before deciding how to take title. California taxes California-source rental income for nonresidents, and withholding rules can apply if you rent the property. ([ftb.ca.gov](https://www.ftb.ca.gov/pay/withholding/withholding-on-nonresidents.html?utm_source=openai)) If you later sell as a foreign person, federal FIRPTA withholding can apply; California has separate real-estate withholding rules as well. ([irs.gov](https://www.irs.gov/individuals/international-taxpayers/firpta-withholding?utm_source=openai)) Depending on your country of residence and the property's value, U.S. estate-tax considerations can also make the choice between personal ownership, an LLC, trust, or another structure important.

If you tell me 1) what country you're a citizen/resident of, 2) roughly how much the LA property would cost, 3) cash or mortgage, and 4) whether it will be your residence, vacation home, or rental, I can lay out the specific requirements and likely taxes/closing costs for your situation.
